reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The work by Machida et al. highlights the development of a novel LSD1 inhibitor (TAS1440) and demonstrate its potential efficacy in small cell lung cancer. The work on the validation of the drug, including its mechanism of action, the exertion of its effect through INSM1 and the connection to NOTCH signaling is very convincing. The authors have done an excellent job of characterizing a novel epigenetic modifier.
Where the manuscript struggles, however, is the focus on small cell lung cancer. That is not to say that small cell lung cancer is not a worthy target of this focus – quite the contrary – but the authors familiarity with small cell lung cancer appears outdated and the manuscript’s impact suffers mightily from this. There has been significant progress in small cell lung cancer – both preclinical and clinically – in the past 3-4 years and the authors seem completely unaware of this, as evidenced by the fact that their most recent citation for small cell lung cancer is the Ireland et al. Cancer Cell manuscript from 2020. This includes even recent publications on LSD1 inhibition in small cell lung cancer (e.g. Nguyen et al. J Thorac Oncol 2022).
Despite the limitations in the authors command of the SCLC literature, there is a convincing case that the activity of TAS1440 is most robust in the neuroendocrine-high subtypes, especially SCLC-A. Their in vitro and in vivo data support this well.
Significant small cell lung cancer-focused revisions to text and experiments would be necessary, in my opinion, to make this a valid addition to the small cell lung cancer body of literature, including:
Major Issues:
(1) The authors focus on the SCLC subtyping proposed by Rudin et al. It should be noted that this was a review and no longer reflects the consensus subtyping approach. In particular, while Rudin et al. proposed YAP1 as a subtype-defining transcription factor, this has been largely dismissed, including from work by Dr. Rudin’s group (see Baine et al. J Thorac Oncol 2020), as well as Gay et al. Cancer Cell 2021 and Ng et al., Clin Cancer Res, 2024. In particular, the three cell lines chosen by the authors here to represent the supposed SCLC-Y subtype were shown in the Ng et al. manuscript to be SMARCA4-deficient undifferentiated tumor in two cases and a sarcomatoid spindle cell neoplasm in the other case (see Table 1). At minimum, the figures should be revised to exclude these cell lines and the SCLC-Y subtype completely.
(2) Once the authors appropriately reconcile their subtypes in Figure 1 and beyond with the current state of the SCLC literature, an key, overlooked direction is how LSD1 inhibition impacts the subtype landscape. This has, to a degree, already been addressed for earlier LSD1 inhibitors – see Nguyen et al. manuscript referenced above. It’s not clear why the authors seem to ignore this manuscript, rather than follow its format and experiments to highlight the ways in which their LSD1 inhibitor may be superior.
a. The authors make no mention of SCLC-I, the inflamed fourth subtype of SCLC. The earlier work by Nguyen et al. suggests that LSD1 inhibition can shift uninflamed, neuroendocrine high SCLC (e.g. SCLC-A) to a more inflamed state reminiscent of SCLC-I. This would be critical to explore here.
b. Do the tumors that are SCLC-A and effectively treated with TAS1440 shift to SCLC-N? SCLC-P? SCLC-I? ASCL1 goes down, but what arises as a result? Even YAP1 is a possibility here, as demonstrated previously by Ireland et al. (which the authors do cite).
c. As LSD1 inhibitors are unlikely to serve as successful single-agent therapies in SCLC, the possibility of combination therapies and the rationale for them is underexplored. If the tumors become more inflamed, could this agent be combined with immune checkpoint blockade? That experiment may be beyond the scope of the publication due to requirement for immunocompetent models, but at least some data supporting more inflammatory features (MHC expression, IFN-y, etc. a la Nguyen et al.) would be appropriate.
d. Combinations with chemotherapies? Impact on expression of high-profile targets (e.g. DLL3 – the target of tarlatamab – or several ADC targets including B7H3, SEZ6, TROP2). Maybe it’s not a good thing to downregulate ASCL1 (and, presumably, DLL3 and SEZ6) since the standard of care for SCLC is now tarlatamab.
(3) In the final paragraph of the results, the authors shift to NSCLC for survival analysis. This is clearly not appropriate to support the implications of targeting LSD1 in SCLC-A. Despite the authors comments, there are data available with transcriptional and clinical data for SCLC, including George et al. Nature 2015, Nabet et al. Cancer Cell 2024, and several others. If the authors wish to include clinical data, they need to gain access to one of several publicly available SCLC datasets.
Minor Issues:
(1) Page 6, line 102. Should this read “potently” rather than “potentially”?
(2) Figure 2B would be easier to interpret if the cell line subtypes were labeled.
(3) The in-text reference for Figure 2D arrives after the in-text reference for Figure 2E.
(4) Page 15, line 317 seems to contain a typographical error “and GSK2879552”.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
In this manuscript, Machida et al. studied the therapeutic effect and understand the mechanism of the new LSD1 inhibitor TAS1440 in neuroendocrine SCLC. Earlier studies showed that LSD1 inhibition derepresses notch and TGFb signaling resulting in suppression of SCLC growth. This study presents the first development of a new LSD1 inhibitor, TAS1440 which is a histone H3 competitive inhibitor of LSD1. TAS1440 demonstrated superior antiproliferative activity in SCLC-A subtype cells and exhibited in vivo activity in subcutaneous xenograft models. Mechanistically, TAS effects are attributed to both direct inhibition of LSD1 enzymatic activity as well as disruption of LSD1-repressive complexes leading to coordinated regulation of histone modifications and activation of transcription factors INSM1 and SMAD2 which reprograms the NOTCH and TGFb tumor suppressor pathways. Further depletion of INSM1 resulted in the abrogation of TAS1440 effects, suggesting the dependency of INSM1 for TAS1440 functions.
This study is interesting as TAS has the dual function of inhibition of LSD1 enzymatic activity and disrupting LSD1 complexes and holds significant promise as a new targeted therapy for the SCLC-A subtype with high INSM1 expression. Data was generated rigorously using multiple cell lines and demonstrated the superior activity of TAS1440 than existing LSD1 inhibitors, and mechanistic studies were thoroughly conducted using RNA-seq of 22 cell lines, as well as ChIP-seq and mass spec studies and rigorous validation in multiple cell lines. The figures are good quality and easy to follow and the manuscript is well written.
However, there are several issues noted in the manuscript and several claims are overstated without concrete evidence. The novelty of the study is moderate as LSD1's role in SCLC, and the utility of other LSD1 inhibitors was thoroughly investigated, although these inhibitors are associated with significant toxicity. The authors claim that TAS1440 has high specificity, less off-target effects, and is a safer drug, which could be a breakthrough for this study. Unfortunately, there was not enough data presented to support this statement. Further the objective states the identification of chemoresistance drivers, however no such studies using chemoresistance cells were conducted. In vivo studies are preliminary in nature, and only one subcutaneous xenograft model was used.
The on-target specificity of the compound should be established using LSD1-KO cells. Further, it is not clear if TAS1440 directly interacts with LSD1. This can be done using biotin-labeled TAS-1440 and LSD1 protein using avidin pulldown.
In vivo studies are conducted using subcutaneous models which do not mimic the actual microenvironment. Only one xenograft model was used. Studies using orthotopic models of SCLC and syngenic models with intact immune systems should be conducted to establish the superior activity of TAS1440. Further, there are no PDX models were utilized to account for the heterogeneity of SCLC.
There were no details provided pertaining to how the in vivo dose of TAS1440 was determined, what its MTD, MED. Concerning toxicity, it appears that this compound also reduces body weight, suspecting the potential toxicity of this compound. It is important to study whether this compound has any hematologic toxicity as commonly observed with other LSD1 inhibitors.
TAS has dual activity of LSD1 enzymatic inhibition and complex disruptor. However, it is essential to determine if the enzymatic activity is important for TAS effects. Efficacy and mechanistic studies need to be conducted using enzymatic dead mutant LSD1 (K661A) to ascertain whether enzymatic activity is essential for TAS1440 effects.
It is not clear how it is different from existing reversible noncovalent inhibitors such as SP2509.
Some of the data was generated using only one cell line, particularly Figure 4g,h,j,k. and 6d,e. This should be done using at least one more cell line.
Authors claim that TAS1440 dissociates TFs such as INSM1 and SMAD2 from the LSD1 complex and synergistically promotes the activation of key signaling pathways such as NOTCH and TGF-b via epigenetic reprogramming. However, no data was provided to support this conclusion except cell viability data.
Data shows that TAS dissociates LSD1 interaction with INSM1 and SMAD2. However, much of the studies are conducted with only INSM1 manipulation. It is not clear what is the role of SMAD2 in TAS actions.
IP data show that in addition to TAS, ORY-1001, and GSK2879552 also reduce the LSD1 interaction with INSM1 despite the latter being catalytic inhibitors. How do the authors explain this? How is TAS1440's superior activity justified here?
Studies that address the molecular basis of resistance using INSM1-KO need to be verified using reexpression of INSM1 in INSM1-KO background and show that reinstating INSM1 expression restores TAS1440 efficacy.
Figure 7I has no significance as this data was generated using NSCLC. I think this data can be removed from the manuscript as earlier studies have already demonstrated the LSD1 survival correlation in NSCLC.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_5:
This manuscript describes a new LSD1 (histone demethylase) inhibitor and its potential pharmacological activity against a sub-type of small-cell lung cancer. The bottom line is that the LSD1 inhibitor disrupts the interaction between the demethylase and INSM1. In this way, this transcription factor looses its ability to function as a repressor of NOTCH and TGF-β signaling. These pathways are thereby activated and induce an epigenetic reprogramming that halts cell proliferation. The authors must be congratulated for the extensive amount of work that they describe in this submission. The experiments are extremely well illustrated and described by the narrative. My enthusiasm is, however, considerably decreased by the consideration that the manuscript almost ignores previous literature. TAS1440, the hereby reported inhibitor, is chemically very similar to CC-90011, a non covalent inhibitor described 15 years ago (10.1021/acs.jmedchem.0c00978) that was moved forwards to clinical trials (doi.org/10.1021/acs.jmedchem.3c02133). Moreover, there is already quite some literature describing the interplay between INSM1 and LSD1 in SCLC. For instance, doi.org/10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-16-3502 shows that inhibition of the LSD1-INSM1 interaction "inhibits expression of neuroendocrine-associated genes, such as ASCL1", anticipating the conclusion of this work. Similar conclusions were given in reference 10 whereas reference 24 demonstrates that "T-3775440 (an irreversible LSD1 inhibitor) blocks proliferation of SCLC cells in vitro and retards SCLC tumor growth in vivo. T-3775440 disrupts the interaction between LSD1 and the transcriptional repressor INSM1, thereby inhibiting expression of neuroendocrine-associated genes, such as ASCL1. INSM1 silencing phenocopies the effects of T-3775440 on gene expression and cell proliferation, consistent with the likelihood T-3775440 mediated its effects in SCLC by inhibiting INSM1". These are virtually the same take-home message offered by this manuscript. The relevance is this work is the demonstration that stratification of the cancer sub-type is critical and that the levels of ASCL1 can be prognostic. The manuscript rationalizes this phenomenon describing a plausible molecular mechanism.
Whether this manuscript meets the degree of novelty expected by the journal is an editorial decision. I recommend that the Authors extensively revise their manuscript highlighting their new findings while properly referring to and comparing with previous work whenever this is relevant. I think that it would be important to compare TAS1440 with CC-90011 with regard to their antiproliferative activity and cell-type selectivity. Given their structural similarity, it may well be possible that they behave the same or with only marginal differences.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We would like to thank Reviewer #1 for their careful and expert appraisal from the perspectives of targeted therapy, drug resistance, and ChIP‑seq. We have undertaken a substantial revision to address the points raised, including (i) standardizing the cell‑growth calculation and updating all affected figures, (ii) adding in vivo efficacy across multiple SCLC‑A models, (iii) strengthening on‑target specificity with LSD1 knockout and catalytic‑dead rescue, (iv) mechanistic clarifications with ChIP/ChIP‑seq and co‑IP, and (v) survival analyses in SCLC (including SCLC‑A). Please refer to our point‑by‑point responses below.
#1-1
1.In Fig. 2a-b, the method used to calculate cell growth (%) is weird (Lines 539-546). The authors tend to exaggerate the impacts of inhibitors using two different formula dependent on the cell number of treatment groups when compared to the control.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. We agree that our original calculation of “cell growth (%)”—which switched between two formulas when post‑treatment cell numbers fell below the initial seeding density—could inflate apparent inhibition, particularly at high doses with substantial cytotoxicity. To eliminate this ambiguity and ensure consistent comparability across conditions, we have adopted a single definition throughout the manuscript:
Cell growth (%) = (cell number in each drug treatment group / cell number in DMSO control group) × 100.
We have recalculated and updated all affected figures and legends (e.g., revised Fig. 2a–d; Fig. S2a, b; Fig. S3a; and other panels quantifying growth inhibition) and revised the Methods accordingly. This uniform approach aligns with standard practice, improves clarity and reproducibility, and does not change the study’s main conclusions. For transparency, we now also clarify in the Methods how values are interpreted under strongly cytotoxic conditions and provide the exact time‑points and seeding parameters used for normalization.
#1-2
2.The authors proposed that TAS1440 could serve as a therapeutic option for SCLC, particularly for the SCLC-A subtype with high INSM1 expression. While their data showed that several SCLC-A cell lines were sensitive to TAS1440, some other SCLC-A lines, including NCI-H69, DMS79, SHP-77, and NCI-H2081, appear resistant to TAS1440 (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 2a). What are the potential mechanisms underlying the differential responses among different subtype-A cell lines to TAS1440 treatment? Could this variability be related to the differences of baseline INSM1 levels, or attributed to the variations of NOTCH or TGF-β signaling activity?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful question. To understand why a subset of SCLC-A lines remains refractory to TAS1440, we stratified our panel into TAS1440-sensitive vs. -insensitive groups by dose–response behavior (revised Fig. 3a) and examined baseline and on-treatment features that track with drug response.
(i) Target abundance (baseline).
Across the full panel and within SCLC-A, KDM1A/LSD1 expression was significantly higher in the insensitive group (revised Fig. 3c), consistent with reduced effective target engagement for an H3-substrate-competitive inhibitor at standard doses. In contrast, baseline INSM1 (and ASCL1) did not differ between sensitive and insensitive SCLC-A lines—likely reflecting uniformly high expression within this lineage (Fig. R1 for Reviewer).
(ii) On-treatment derepression capacity.
Drug response correlated strongly with the magnitude of INSM1 downregulation on treatment (ΔINSM1) rather than with baseline INSM1 (revised Fig. 3f; correlation statistics are reported in the legend). Consistently, GSEA of RNA-seq after TAS1440 showed NOTCH pathway enrichment in sensitive lines (both across the panel and within SCLC-A), whereas TGF-β enrichment was not consistently different between groups (revised Fig. 3d; Fig. R1 for reviewer). These data support a model in which TAS1440 efficacy appears to require the ability to derepress NOTCH signaling downstream of LSD1 inhibition in an INSM1-high neuroendocrine context.
(iii) Functional perturbations.
INSM1 knockdown in two sensitive SCLC-A lines (NCI-H1417, NCI-H510A) reduced TAS1440 sensitivity (revised Fig. S13j, k). Conversely, INSM1 overexpression in two resistant non-neuroendocrine lines (NCI-H211/SCLC-P and NCI-H196/SMARCA4-deficient) increased TAS1440 sensitivity and induced NE features (revised Fig. S17a–j). In the resistant SCLC-A line DMS79, ectopic INSM1 increased TAS1440-responsive DEGs and yielded partial post-treatment activation of both pathways (revised Fig. S17e–j).
Conclusion.
Heterogeneous TAS1440 sensitivity within SCLC-A appears to reflect a combination of (1) target abundance (higher LSD1 dampens a substrate-competitive inhibitor) and (2) on-treatment derepression competence—specifically, the ability to downregulate INSM1 and reactivate NOTCH upon LSD1 inhibition. This framework explains why several SCLC-A lines (e.g., NCI-H69, DMS79, SHP-77, NCI-H2081) are less responsive despite shared lineage identity. Full statistics (effect sizes, n, tests, and P-val) are provided in the revised figure legends; definitions of sensitive/insensitive and dose–response modeling are detailed in the Methods.
#1-3.
3. In Fig. 5g, what is the difference between the left and right panels? They seem identical.
Response: Thank you for pointing this out. Originally, this figure was designed to appear three-dimensional, but it has been changed to a standard two-dimensional structure to avoid confusion. Please refer to the revised Fig. 5i.
#1-4
4. Only one cell line is used to evaluate the efficacy of TAS1440 in vivo (Fig. 7j). At least two should be studied.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important suggestion. In response, we have broadened our in‑vivo evaluation beyond the original NCI‑H1417 model to include three additional SCLC‑A xenograft models—NCI‑H146, NCI‑H510A, COR‑L51 and a INSM1 knockout (KO) NCI-H146 xenograft model. TAS1440 significantly suppressed tumor growth across all SCLC-A additional models (revised Fig. 9a-e; Fig. 9g and Fig. S18e, i), consistent with our initial H1417 findings (revised Fig. 9a), whereas INSM1 knockout (KO) NCI-H146 xenografts were non responsive (revised Fig. 9f). To address microenvironmental relevance, we have conducted an orthotopic study by implanting SCLC‑A cells into the lung parenchyma. TAS1440 treatment markedly lowered intrathoracic tumor burden. CT imaging revealed a 66.7% reduction in tumor area at the maximal radius (revised Fig.9k). These concordant results strengthen the generalizability of TAS1440’s in‑vivo efficacy within SCLC‑A and support its subtype‑selective therapeutic potential. Details of dose, schedule, sample size, randomization/blinding, effect sizes with 95% CIs, and statistical tests are reported in the revised figure legends and Methods sections.
The following text has been added to the manuscript (Results):
“To evaluate the in‑vivo efficacy of TAS1440, we assessed tumor growth inhibition in xenograft mouse models derived from four SCLC‑A cell lines (NCI‑H1417, NCI‑H146, NCI‑H510A, COR‑L51). TAS1440 treatment significantly reduced tumor volume vs. vehicle across all models (Fig. 9a-e; Fig. 9g and Fig. S18e, i).” Study design parameters (dose/schedule), randomization and blinding procedures, n, and statistical analyses are provided in the figure legends and Methods.
#1-5
5. In Fig. 7l, the authors assessed the prognostic value of KDM1A, NOTCH1 and TGFB2 in NSCLC but not SCLC patients. To strengthen their conclusions, the authors should perform survival analyses using SCLC datasets. Although clinical data for SCLC are limited, studies with larger sample sizes of SCLC with RNA-seq data are available (PMID: 38181741; PMID: 27093186). Moreover, since the authors concluded that “This demonstrates the prognostic and therapeutic implications of targeting the INSM1-LSD1 complex in small cell lung cancer, particularly in SCLC-A subtype” (Lines 420-422), it would be ideal to evaluate these survival analyses specifically in the SCLC-A subtype. The evaluation of prognostic implications of INSM1 in SCLC would also be informative.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. In response, we have removed the prior NSCLC‑based analysis and performed overall‑survival analyses in a publicly available SCLC RNA‑seq cohort (Liu et al. 2024; PMID: 38181741).
In the entire SCLC cohort, higher KDM1A (LSD1) expression was significantly associated with shorter overall survival, supporting its potential prognostic relevance (revised Fig. 9l). By contrast, lower INSM1 showed a trend toward longer survival that did not reach statistical significance in the overall cohort (revised Fig. 9l).
To address the request for subtype‑restricted evaluation, we analyzed the SCLC‑A subgroup defined by an ASCL1‑high transcriptional program, consistent with current consensus. Directionally similar trends were observed for both KDM1A and INSM1, but associations did not reach statistical significance, likely reflecting limited power within subtype‑restricted strata (revised Fig. 9m). These findings are directionally concordant with prior pathology‑based reports linking lower INSM1/LSD1 expression to better outcomes in SCLC (Sakakibara R, et al. Am J Surg Pathol 44:757-764,2020., Xu et al. Pathol Res Pract;229:153693,2022.).
For transparency, we now restrict clinical inferences to SCLC datasets. Analytic details were pre‑specified: median expression cut‑offs, Kaplan–Meier log‑rank tests, and Cox models reporting hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals; multiple‑testing control is indicated in the figure legends and Methods sections. We note the inherent limitations of available resources (lack of uniform pretreatment/response annotation, bulk RNA‑seq averaging of intra‑tumoral heterogeneity, and modest sample sizes for subtype‑specific analyses). While clinical prognostication is not the primary aim of this mechanistic work, these results support—but do not overstate—the clinical relevance of the INSM1–LSD1 axis in SCLC, particularly within SCLC‑A.
#1-6
6. Fig. s8e showed that TAS1440-induced NOTCH1 upregulation was significantly impaired in INSM1-deficient cells (lane 3), suggesting that INSM1 is required for TAS1440-induced NOTCH1 upregulation. However, the same data also showed that NOTCH1 expression was markedly upregulated in INSM1-deficient cells without TAS1440 treatment (lane 2), indicative a suppressive role of INSM1 in NOTCH1 induction. How do the authors reconcile these seemingly contradictory effects of INSM1 on NOTCH1 expression?
Response: We appreciate this incisive question and agree that the observations can be reconciled within a single, context‑dependent derepression model. Under basal conditions, INSM1 tethers an LSD1‑containing corepressor complex, establishing a poised repressive state over tumor‑suppressive programs such as NOTCH and TGF‑β. Accordingly, loss of INSM1 derepresses these loci, elevating baseline NOTCH1 (revised Fig. S14e, lane 2) by removing the repressive scaffold. Upon TAS1440 exposure, inhibition of LSD1 catalytic activity together with disruption of the INSM1–LSD1 complex lifts repression and induces pathway activation. However, in INSM1‑deficient cells, the TAS‑sensitive repressive complex is already absent; baseline NOTCH1 is partially elevated, and the dynamic range for further TAS‑mediated induction is reduced, yielding the attenuated upregulation observed (revised Fig. S14e, lane 3).
Consistent with this model, INSM1 knockdown did not alter H3K4me1/2/3 at TSSs, whereas H3K27ac was significantly increased, indicating release of repression; NOTCH1 and TGFB2 showed corresponding increases in H3K27ac and transcript levels (revised Fig. 8n–r). Baseline repression is further supported by INSM1‑overexpression experiments in H196 and DMS79, where ectopic INSM1 enhanced TAS1440‑induced increases in pSMAD2 and the induction of NOTCH1, albeit with cell line-dependent variation. (revised Fig. S17g-h, lane3 vs. lane1).
Together, these data support INSM1 acting primarily as a chromatin‑tethered repressor at these loci, with TAS1440 functioning by derepressing INSM1/LSD1‑programmed sites. This framework parsimoniously explains both (i) the baseline NOTCH1 increase upon INSM1 loss and (ii) the blunted incremental induction by TAS1440 in the absence of INSM1.
To improve clarity, we have (i) added baseline and on‑treatment NOTCH1 quantification (fold‑change, effect sizes, and P values) to illustrate the dynamic‑range effect and (ii) revised the text to explicitly state this derepression model (revised Fig. S14d–e; Results, pp. 23–24).
#1-7
7. The authors stated that “TAS1440 treatment resulted in the dissociation of 78 nuclear factors, of which 13 were epigenetic factors, from LSD1 (Fig. 5c, red)” (Lines 264-266). However, only 6 genes are labeled in red in Fig. 5c.
Response: Thank you for drawing this to our attention. We agree that the labeling in the original (former) Fig. 5c was not sufficiently clear. In the revised Fig. 5c, all 13 epigenetic factors that dissociate from LSD1 upon TAS1440 exposure are now consistently highlighted in red, matching the statement in the text. To aid interpretation, we have boxed the five interactors prioritized for experimental validation (INSM1, SMAD2, HDAC1, HDAC2, RCOR1). As shown by the accompanying co‑immunoprecipitation/immunoblot analyses (revised Fig. 5e, f), these proteins indeed dissociate from LSD1 following TAS1440 treatment.
For transparency, the figure legend now defines the color/box annotations and specifies the criteria for “dissociation” (significance threshold and fold‑change), and the Source Data file lists the full set of 78 nuclear factors and the 13 epigenetic factors.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author): An early career researcher co-reviewer
I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
Response: We appreciate Nature Communications’ Early Career Researcher co‑review initiative and thank the co‑reviewer for their contribution.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author): neuroendocrine SCLC and targeted therapy
The work by Machida et al. highlights the development of a novel LSD1 inhibitor (TAS1440) and demonstrate its potential efficacy in small cell lung cancer. The work on the validation of the drug, including its mechanism of action, the exertion of its effect through INSM1 and the connection to NOTCH signaling is very convincing. The authors have done an excellent job of characterizing a novel epigenetic modifier.
Where the manuscript struggles, however, is the focus on small cell lung cancer. That is not to say that small cell lung cancer is not a worthy target of this focus – quite the contrary – but the authors familiarity with small cell lung cancer appears outdated and the manuscript’s impact suffers mightily from this. There has been significant progress in small cell lung cancer – both preclinical and clinically – in the past 3-4 years and the authors seem completely unaware of this, as evidenced by the fact that their most recent citation for small cell lung cancer is the Ireland et al. Cancer Cell manuscript from 2020. This includes even recent publications on LSD1 inhibition in small cell lung cancer (e.g. Nguyen et al. J Thorac Oncol 2022). Despite the limitations in the authors command of the SCLC literature, there is a convincing case that the activity of TAS1440 is most robust in the neuroendocrine-high subtypes, especially SCLC-A. Their in vitro and in vivo data support this well.
Significant small cell lung cancer-focused revisions to text and experiments would be necessary, in my opinion, to make this a valid addition to the small cell lung cancer body of literature, including:
Response: We sincerely appreciate the constructive critique and agree that our initial submission did not sufficiently reflect recent advances in SCLC biology and therapy. We have therefore comprehensively realigned the manuscript to current consensus by:
 Updating SCLC subtyping (restricting to SCLC-A/N/P, removing the legacy SCLC-Y/SMARCA4-deficientlines from canonical analyses per recent reports) and revising the figures accordingly (from revised Fig. 2 onward).
 Expanding in-vivo validation beyond H1417 to three additional SCLC-A xenografts (revised Fig. 9). Consistent antitumor activity was also confirmed in an orthotopic lung model.
 Replacing the prior NSCLC survival panel with SCLC-only overall-survival analyses, including SCLC-A–restricted evaluation (Liu et al., 2024; PMID: 38181741; revised Fig. 9l, m).
 Strengthening on-target and mechanistic evidence (LSD1 KO dependency; WT/K661A rescue; complex disruption; epigenomic readouts).
 Reframing the work within the modern SCLC literature, explicitly integrating Nguyen et al. (JTO 2022) and other key studies (Baine 2020; Gay 2021; Ng 2024; George 2015; Nabet 2024) into the Introduction/Discussion.
 Where appropriate, we now discuss SCLC-I–related inflammatory programs and the rationale for ICB combinations in the context of LSD1 inhibition.
Please refer to our detailed, point-by-point responses below.
Major Issues:
#3-1
(1) The authors focus on the SCLC subtyping proposed by Rudin et al. It should be noted that this was a review and no longer reflects the consensus subtyping approach. In particular, while Rudin et al. proposed YAP1 as a subtype-defining transcription factor, this has been largely dismissed, including from work by Dr. Rudin’s group (see Baine et al. J Thorac Oncol 2020), as well as Gay et al. Cancer Cell 2021 and Ng et al., Clin Cancer Res, 2024. In particular, the three cell lines chosen by the authors here to represent the supposed SCLC-Y subtype were shown in the Ng et al. manuscript to be SMARCA4-deficient undifferentiated tumor in two cases and a sarcomatoid spindle cell neoplasm in the other case (see Table 1). At minimum, the figures should be revised to exclude these cell lines and the SCLC-Y subtype completely.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We agree that the YAP1‑defined “SCLC‑Y” category proposed in the 2019 review by Rudin et al. no longer reflects current consensus. Subsequent studies—including Baine et al. (J Thorac Oncol, 2020), Gay et al. (Cancer Cell, 2021), and Ng et al. (Clin Cancer Res, 2024; Table 1)—indicate that cell lines historically labeled “SCLC‑Y” were misclassified, corresponding instead to SMARCA4‑deficient undifferentiated tumors or sarcomatoid spindle‑cell neoplasms. In line with this literature, we re‑examined our transcriptomic data and confirmed markedly reduced SMARCA4 expression in the previously designated SCLC‑Y lines (revised Fig. 1e), supporting their exclusion from canonical SCLC analyses.
Accordingly, we have removed the SCLC‑Y subtype and all associated cell lines from downstream analyses. From revised Fig. 2 onward, we focus exclusively on the currently recognized subtypes—SCLC‑A, SCLC‑N, and SCLC‑P—and have updated all figures, legends, and text to align with this framework. For transparency, we provide a supplementary table listing included/excluded cell lines with the rationale for each decision (Supplementary Table S3). We believe these revisions improve rigor, interpretability, and alignment with contemporary SCLC biology.
#3-1-a
(2) Once the authors appropriately reconcile their subtypes in Figure 1 and beyond with the current state of the SCLC literature, an key, overlooked direction is how LSD1 inhibition impacts the subtype landscape. This has, to a degree, already been addressed for earlier LSD1 inhibitors – see Nguyen et al. manuscript referenced above. It’s not clear why the authors seem to ignore this manuscript, rather than follow its format and experiments to highlight the ways in which their LSD1 inhibitor may be superior.
a. The authors make no mention of SCLC-I, the inflamed fourth subtype of SCLC. The earlier work by Nguyen et al. suggests that LSD1 inhibition can shift uninflamed, neuroendocrine high SCLC (e.g. SCLC-A) to a more inflamed state reminiscent of SCLC-I. This would be critical to explore here.
Response: Thank you for this insightful suggestion. We fully acknowledge the clinical relevance of the inflamed SCLC‑I subtype and prior evidence that LSD1 inhibition can shift neuroendocrine‑high states (e.g., SCLC‑A) toward a more inflamed phenotype (Nguyen et al., J Thorac Oncol 2022). Because SCLC‑I designation relies on tumor–immune context (immune‑cell infiltration, IFN‑γ pathway activity, antigen presentation)—features not faithfully recapitulated in 2D cell‑line systems—we did not assign an SCLC‑I label in vitro to avoid over‑interpretation.
Nevertheless, we have adopted an analytic framework consistent with Nguyen et al. and systematically queried immunologic rewiring under TAS1440. We have also profiled canonical markers (IFNG, CXCL9/CXCL10, HLA‑A/B/C, B2M, TAP1/TAP2, STAT1, IRF1, CD274/PD‑L1) and performed GSEA on RNA‑seq data. TAS1440 decreased CD274 (PD‑L1) while increasing MHC‑I components (e.g., B2M) and IFN‑γ–responsive genes (e.g., IRF1); inflammatory signatures were activated in a subset of lines, although unsupervised clustering did not yield a robust SCLC‑I‑like group in vitro (revised Fig. S9d, f). Where applicable, NES and P values are reported in the figure legend to aid interpretation. Importantly, a decrease in PD‑L1 transcripts does not preclude enhanced immunogenicity when antigen‑presentation and IFN‑γ programs increase concurrently, which can raise tumor visibility to cytotoxic T cells.
Taken together, while TAS1440 induces MHC‑I/IFN‑γ–responsive genes in a subset of lines (for example, B2M, TAP1/2, IRF1; Fig. S9d, f), strict assignment to the SCLC‑I subtype is not possible in vitro using bulk RNA‑seq. We therefore avoided SCLC‑I labeling and instead reported pathway‑level changes with appropriate caveats. Future work will test orthotopic/PDX and immune co‑culture models to evaluate ICB combinations with predefined pharmacodynamic readouts. We have added these analyses and a tempered discussion to the revised manuscript (Results/Methods/Discussion; revised Fig. S9d, f).
#3-1-b
b. Do the tumors that are SCLC-A and effectively treated with TAS1440 shift to SCLC-N? SCLC-P? SCLC-I? ASCL1 goes down, but what arises as a result? Even YAP1 is a possibility here, as demonstrated previously by Ireland et al. (which the authors do cite).
Response: Thank you for this thoughtful question on subtype plasticity after TAS1440. Across multiple SCLC‑A cell lines, TAS1440 consistently downregulated ASCL1 and INSM1, consistent with disruption of the LSD1–INSM1–ASCL1 axis. To determine whether this suppression precipitates a lineage switch, we have profiled subtype‑defining programs—NEUROD1 (SCLC‑N), POU2F3 (SCLC‑P), and YAP1 activity (assessed as a pathway readout rather than as a distinct “SCLC‑Y” subtype)—before and after TAS1440 (revised Fig. S9a). We did not observe reproducible induction of NEUROD1, POU2F3, or YAP1‑associated signatures. Unsupervised clustering based on canonical marker sets likewise indicated that overall transcriptional identity remained largely stable, with no coordinated transition from SCLC‑A to other subtypes (revised Fig. S9b, c; enrichment statistics are reported in the legend).
As these experiments reflect short‑term (≤7‑day) in‑vitro exposure, delayed plasticity under chronic dosing and/or microenvironmental cues cannot be excluded. Within the tested window, TAS1440‑mediated ASCL1 suppression attenuates the neuroendocrine program but does not, by itself, drive a switch to SCLC‑N, SCLC‑P, or an SCLC‑I‑like state. These results and their limitations have been incorporated into the revised Results/Discussion (revised Fig. S9a–c).
#3-2-c
c. As LSD1 inhibitors are unlikely to serve as successful single-agent therapies in SCLC, the possibility of combination therapies and the rationale for them is underexplored. If the tumors become more inflamed, could this agent be combined with immune checkpoint blockade? That experiment may be beyond the scope of the publication due to requirement for immunocompetent models, but at least some data supporting more inflammatory features (MHC expression, IFN-y, etc. a la Nguyen et al.) would be appropriate.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. We agree that LSD1 inhibitors are unlikely to deliver durable benefit as monotherapies in SCLC and that rational combinations—particularly those leveraging immunologic reprogramming—are essential for translation. Prior reports (e.g., Nguyen et al., J Thorac Oncol 2022; Lin et al., Cell Reports 2024) have shown that LSD1 inhibition can enhance antigen‑presentation programs and IFN‑γ–responsive transcription.
To assess whether TAS1440 elicits similar effects, we analyzed RNA‑seq from 19 SCLC cell lines and profiled MHC‑I components, IFN‑γ signaling, and immune‑checkpoint genes after treatment. TAS1440 downregulated CD274 (PD‑L1) while upregulating MHC‑I pathway genes (e.g., B2M) and IFN‑γ–responsive genes (e.g., IRF1) (revised Fig. S9d). Gene‑set enrichment analysis further showed activation of inflammatory/immune‑related signatures in a subset of models (revised Fig. S9f); NES and FDR values are reported in the legend. As expected in cell‑line systems lacking an intact tumor–immune microenvironment, these changes were not uniformly correlated with growth sensitivity; however, they are consistent with a shift toward greater antigen‑presentation capacity, even with decreased PD‑L1 transcripts.
Consistent with this concept, studies of other reversible LSD1 inhibitors (e.g., Bomedemstat, SP‑2577, CC‑90011) reported increased CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration, induction of IFN‑γ–related genes, and improved responses to anti–PD‑1 in preclinical settings. Although direct combination experiments are beyond the scope of our current in‑vitro study, these transcriptomic data (revised Fig. S9d, f) provide a mechanistic rationale to test TAS1440 + immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) in microenvironment‑preserving systems (orthotopic, syngeneic, or humanized/PDX), with prespecified pharmacodynamic endpoints (MHC‑I upregulation, IFN‑γ‑response gene induction, intratumoral CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration) and objective tumor‑control readouts. We have added these data and an expanded discussion to the revised manuscript.
#3-2-d
d. Combinations with chemotherapies? Impact on expression of high-profile targets (e.g. DLL3 – the target of b – or several ADC targets including B7H3, SEZ6, TROP2). Maybe it’s not a good thing to downregulate ASCL1 (and, presumably, DLL3 and SEZ6) since the standard of care for SCLC is now tarlatamab.
Response: Thank you for raising this important point regarding how TAS1440 may influence clinically actionable surface targets and, by extension, combination strategies.
Using RNA‑seq, we compared expression of relevant antigens before and after TAS1440 (revised Fig. S9e): DLL3 (tarlatamab, a DLL3‑CD3 bispecific T‑cell engager), SEZ6 (investigational ADCs), B7‑H3/CD276 (enoblituzumab, MGC018), and TROP2/TACSTD2 (sacituzumab govitecan). Across multiple SCLC‑A lines, TAS1440 significantly downregulated DLL3, whereas SEZ6, CD276 (B7‑H3), and TACSTD2 (TROP2) remained largely unchanged across SCLC‑A lines (revised Fig. S9e). Consistent with DLL3 being downstream of ASCL1, which itself is suppressed by LSD1 inhibition, NOTCH pathway enrichment (NES) negatively correlated with ASCL1 and DLL3 fold changes (R = −0.66 and R = −0.63, respectively; Fig. S9g). This aligns with our mechanistic model whereby TAS1440 disrupts the LSD1–INSM1–ASCL1 axis and indirectly activates NOTCH signaling. In contrast, SEZ6, B7‑H3, and TROP2 were largely unchanged after TAS1440, suggesting these ADC targets may remain exploitable in combination regimens (summary statistics are reported in the legend).
Practical implications: Because DLL3 declines under TAS1440, concurrent TAS1440–tarlatamab administration is unlikely to be optimal. A more rational approach would be sequencing—deploying tarlatamab when DLL3 expression is highest and reserving TAS1440 for windows aimed at transcriptional reprogramming—rather than simultaneous dosing. More broadly, the relative stability of SEZ6, B7‑H3, and TROP2 supports the feasibility of ADC‑based combinations that do not rely on DLL3 while TAS1440 is on board. We note that these are transcript‑level observations; surface protein levels were not directly quantified here.
Regarding chemotherapy combinations, although outside the scope of the present work, future studies could evaluate TAS1440 with standard cytotoxics (e.g., platinum–etoposide or topotecan), using prespecified synergy metrics and schedule optimization, while monitoring pharmacodynamic markers (ASCL1/DLL3 modulation, DNA‑damage/repair signatures) and non‑overlapping toxicity. These considerations provide a clear framework for biomarker‑guided sequencing and combination strategies in SCLC.
#3-3
(3) In the final paragraph of the results, the authors shift to NSCLC for survival analysis. This is clearly not appropriate to support the implications of targeting LSD1 in SCLC-A. Despite the authors comments, there are data available with transcriptional and clinical data for SCLC, including George et al. Nature 2015, Nabet et al. Cancer Cell 2024, and several others. If the authors wish to include clinical data, they need to gain access to one of several publicly available SCLC datasets.
Response: We appreciate this thoughtful comment. In response, we removed the prior NSCLC‑based analysis and performed overall survival analyses in a publicly available SCLC RNA‑seq cohort (PMID: 38181741). In the full SCLC cohort, higher KDM1A (LSD1) expression was significantly associated with shorter overall survival, supporting the prognostic relevance of LSD1 (revised Fig. 9l). By contrast, lower INSM1 expression showed a trend toward improved survival that did not reach statistical significance in the overall cohort (revised Fig. 9l).
To meet the request for subtype‑restricted evaluation, we further analyzed the SCLC‑A subgroup (defined by an ASCL1‑high transcriptional program aligned with current consensus). Directionally similar trends were observed for KDM1A and INSM1, but associations did not reach statistical significance, likely reflecting limited power within subtype‑restricted strata (revised Fig. 9m).
These findings are directionally concordant with prior pathology‑based reports linking lower INSM1/LSD1 expression to better outcomes in SCLC, while differences in cohort composition and therapy may contribute to variability across studies. For transparency, we now restrict all clinical inferences to SCLC datasets. Analytic details were prespecified (median expression cut‑offs; Kaplan–Meier log‑rank tests; Cox proportional‑hazards models reporting hazard ratios with 95% CIs; multiple‑testing control as appropriate), and cohort size/event counts are reported in the figure legends and Methods sections. Although clinical prognostication is not the primary aim of this mechanistic study, future work—where feasible—could extend survival analyses to additional public SCLC resources (e.g., George et al., 2015; Nabet et al., 2024) to further refine the clinical implications of the INSM1–LSD1 axis.
Minor Issues:
(1) Page 6, line 102. Should this read “potently” rather than “potentially”?
