Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We agree that the YAP1‑defined “SCLC‑Y” category proposed in the 2019 review by Rudin et al. no longer reflects current consensus. Subsequent studies—including Baine et al. (J Thorac Oncol, 2020), Gay et al. (Cancer Cell, 2021), and Ng et al. (Clin Cancer Res, 2024; Table 1)—indicate that cell lines historically labeled “SCLC‑Y” were misclassified, corresponding instead to SMARCA4‑deficient undifferentiated tumors or sarcomatoid spindle‑cell neoplasms. In line with this literature, we re‑examined our transcriptomic data and confirmed markedly reduced SMARCA4 expression in the previously designated SCLC‑Y lines (revised Fig. 1e), supporting their exclusion from canonical SCLC analyses.
Accordingly, we have removed the SCLC‑Y subtype and all associated cell lines from downstream analyses. From revised Fig. 2 onward, we focus exclusively on the currently recognized subtypes—SCLC‑A, SCLC‑N, and SCLC‑P—and have updated all figures, legends, and text to align with this framework. For transparency, we provide a supplementary table listing included/excluded cell lines with the rationale for each decision (Supplementary Table S3). We believe these revisions improve rigor, interpretability, and alignment with contemporary SCLC biology.
#3-1-a
(2) Once the authors appropriately reconcile their subtypes in Figure 1 and beyond with the current state of the SCLC literature, an key, overlooked direction is how LSD1 inhibition impacts the subtype landscape. This has, to a degree, already been addressed for earlier LSD1 inhibitors – see Nguyen et al. manuscript referenced above. It’s not clear why the authors seem to ignore this manuscript, rather than follow its format and experiments to highlight the ways in which their LSD1 inhibitor may be superior.
a. The authors make no mention of SCLC-I, the inflamed fourth subtype of SCLC. The earlier work by Nguyen et al. suggests that LSD1 inhibition can shift uninflamed, neuroendocrine high SCLC (e.g. SCLC-A) to a more inflamed state reminiscent of SCLC-I. This would be critical to explore here.
Response: Thank you for this insightful suggestion. We fully acknowledge the clinical relevance of the inflamed SCLC‑I subtype and prior evidence that LSD1 inhibition can shift neuroendocrine‑high states (e.g., SCLC‑A) toward a more inflamed phenotype (Nguyen et al., J Thorac Oncol 2022). Because SCLC‑I designation relies on tumor–immune context (immune‑cell infiltration, IFN‑γ pathway activity, antigen presentation)—features not faithfully recapitulated in 2D cell‑line systems—we did not assign an SCLC‑I label in vitro to avoid over‑interpretation.
Nevertheless, we have adopted an analytic framework consistent with Nguyen et al. and systematically queried immunologic rewiring under TAS1440. We have also profiled canonical markers (IFNG, CXCL9/CXCL10, HLA‑A/B/C, B2M, TAP1/TAP2, STAT1, IRF1, CD274/PD‑L1) and performed GSEA on RNA‑seq data. TAS1440 decreased CD274 (PD‑L1) while increasing MHC‑I components (e.g., B2M) and IFN‑γ–responsive genes (e.g., IRF1); inflammatory signatures were activated in a subset of lines, although unsupervised clustering did not yield a robust SCLC‑I‑like group in vitro (revised Fig. S9d, f). Where applicable, NES and P values are reported in the figure legend to aid interpretation. Importantly, a decrease in PD‑L1 transcripts does not preclude enhanced immunogenicity when antigen‑presentation and IFN‑γ programs increase concurrently, which can raise tumor visibility to cytotoxic T cells.
Taken together, while TAS1440 induces MHC‑I/IFN‑γ–responsive genes in a subset of lines (for example, B2M, TAP1/2, IRF1; Fig. S9d, f), strict assignment to the SCLC‑I subtype is not possible in vitro using bulk RNA‑seq. We therefore avoided SCLC‑I labeling and instead reported pathway‑level changes with appropriate caveats. Future work will test orthotopic/PDX and immune co‑culture models to evaluate ICB combinations with predefined pharmacodynamic readouts. We have added these analyses and a tempered discussion to the revised manuscript (Results/Methods/Discussion; revised Fig. S9d, f).
#3-1-b
b. Do the tumors that are SCLC-A and effectively treated with TAS1440 shift to SCLC-N? SCLC-P? SCLC-I? ASCL1 goes down, but what arises as a result? Even YAP1 is a possibility here, as demonstrated previously by Ireland et al. (which the authors do cite).
Response: Thank you for this thoughtful question on subtype plasticity after TAS1440. Across multiple SCLC‑A cell lines, TAS1440 consistently downregulated ASCL1 and INSM1, consistent with disruption of the LSD1–INSM1–ASCL1 axis. To determine whether this suppression precipitates a lineage switch, we have profiled subtype‑defining programs—NEUROD1 (SCLC‑N), POU2F3 (SCLC‑P), and YAP1 activity (assessed as a pathway readout rather than as a distinct “SCLC‑Y” subtype)—before and after TAS1440 (revised Fig. S9a). We did not observe reproducible induction of NEUROD1, POU2F3, or YAP1‑associated signatures. Unsupervised clustering based on canonical marker sets likewise indicated that overall transcriptional identity remained largely stable, with no coordinated transition from SCLC‑A to other subtypes (revised Fig. S9b, c; enrichment statistics are reported in the legend).
As these experiments reflect short‑term (≤7‑day) in‑vitro exposure, delayed plasticity under chronic dosing and/or microenvironmental cues cannot be excluded. Within the tested window, TAS1440‑mediated ASCL1 suppression attenuates the neuroendocrine program but does not, by itself, drive a switch to SCLC‑N, SCLC‑P, or an SCLC‑I‑like state. These results and their limitations have been incorporated into the revised Results/Discussion (revised Fig. S9a–c).
#3-2-c
c. As LSD1 inhibitors are unlikely to serve as successful single-agent therapies in SCLC, the possibility of combination therapies and the rationale for them is underexplored. If the tumors become more inflamed, could this agent be combined with immune checkpoint blockade? That experiment may be beyond the scope of the publication due to requirement for immunocompetent models, but at least some data supporting more inflammatory features (MHC expression, IFN-y, etc. a la Nguyen et al.) would be appropriate.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. We agree that LSD1 inhibitors are unlikely to deliver durable benefit as monotherapies in SCLC and that rational combinations—particularly those leveraging immunologic reprogramming—are essential for translation. Prior reports (e.g., Nguyen et al., J Thorac Oncol 2022; Lin et al., Cell Reports 2024) have shown that LSD1 inhibition can enhance antigen‑presentation programs and IFN‑γ–responsive transcription.
To assess whether TAS1440 elicits similar effects, we analyzed RNA‑seq from 19 SCLC cell lines and profiled MHC‑I components, IFN‑γ signaling, and immune‑checkpoint genes after treatment. TAS1440 downregulated CD274 (PD‑L1) while upregulating MHC‑I pathway genes (e.g., B2M) and IFN‑γ–responsive genes (e.g., IRF1) (revised Fig. S9d). Gene‑set enrichment analysis further showed activation of inflammatory/immune‑related signatures in a subset of models (revised Fig. S9f); NES and FDR values are reported in the legend. As expected in cell‑line systems lacking an intact tumor–immune microenvironment, these changes were not uniformly correlated with growth sensitivity; however, they are consistent with a shift toward greater antigen‑presentation capacity, even with decreased PD‑L1 transcripts.
Consistent with this concept, studies of other reversible LSD1 inhibitors (e.g., Bomedemstat, SP‑2577, CC‑90011) reported increased CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration, induction of IFN‑γ–related genes, and improved responses to anti–PD‑1 in preclinical settings. Although direct combination experiments are beyond the scope of our current in‑vitro study, these transcriptomic data (revised Fig. S9d, f) provide a mechanistic rationale to test TAS1440 + immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) in microenvironment‑preserving systems (orthotopic, syngeneic, or humanized/PDX), with prespecified pharmacodynamic endpoints (MHC‑I upregulation, IFN‑γ‑response gene induction, intratumoral CD8⁺ T‑cell infiltration) and objective tumor‑control readouts. We have added these data and an expanded discussion to the revised manuscript.
#3-2-d
d. Combinations with chemotherapies? Impact on expression of high-profile targets (e.g. DLL3 – the target of b – or several ADC targets including B7H3, SEZ6, TROP2). Maybe it’s not a good thing to downregulate ASCL1 (and, presumably, DLL3 and SEZ6) since the standard of care for SCLC is now tarlatamab.
Response: Thank you for raising this important point regarding how TAS1440 may influence clinically actionable surface targets and, by extension, combination strategies.
Using RNA‑seq, we compared expression of relevant antigens before and after TAS1440 (revised Fig. S9e): DLL3 (tarlatamab, a DLL3‑CD3 bispecific T‑cell engager), SEZ6 (investigational ADCs), B7‑H3/CD276 (enoblituzumab, MGC018), and TROP2/TACSTD2 (sacituzumab govitecan). Across multiple SCLC‑A lines, TAS1440 significantly downregulated DLL3, whereas SEZ6, CD276 (B7‑H3), and TACSTD2 (TROP2) remained largely unchanged across SCLC‑A lines (revised Fig. S9e). Consistent with DLL3 being downstream of ASCL1, which itself is suppressed by LSD1 inhibition, NOTCH pathway enrichment (NES) negatively correlated with ASCL1 and DLL3 fold changes (R = −0.66 and R = −0.63, respectively; Fig. S9g). This aligns with our mechanistic model whereby TAS1440 disrupts the LSD1–INSM1–ASCL1 axis and indirectly activates NOTCH signaling. In contrast, SEZ6, B7‑H3, and TROP2 were largely unchanged after TAS1440, suggesting these ADC targets may remain exploitable in combination regimens (summary statistics are reported in the legend).
Practical implications: Because DLL3 declines under TAS1440, concurrent TAS1440–tarlatamab administration is unlikely to be optimal. A more rational approach would be sequencing—deploying tarlatamab when DLL3 expression is highest and reserving TAS1440 for windows aimed at transcriptional reprogramming—rather than simultaneous dosing. More broadly, the relative stability of SEZ6, B7‑H3, and TROP2 supports the feasibility of ADC‑based combinations that do not rely on DLL3 while TAS1440 is on board. We note that these are transcript‑level observations; surface protein levels were not directly quantified here.
Regarding chemotherapy combinations, although outside the scope of the present work, future studies could evaluate TAS1440 with standard cytotoxics (e.g., platinum–etoposide or topotecan), using prespecified synergy metrics and schedule optimization, while monitoring pharmacodynamic markers (ASCL1/DLL3 modulation, DNA‑damage/repair signatures) and non‑overlapping toxicity. These considerations provide a clear framework for biomarker‑guided sequencing and combination strategies in SCLC.
#3-3
(3) In the final paragraph of the results, the authors shift to NSCLC for survival analysis. This is clearly not appropriate to support the implications of targeting LSD1 in SCLC-A. Despite the authors comments, there are data available with transcriptional and clinical data for SCLC, including George et al. Nature 2015, Nabet et al. Cancer Cell 2024, and several others. If the authors wish to include clinical data, they need to gain access to one of several publicly available SCLC datasets.
Response: We appreciate this thoughtful comment. In response, we removed the prior NSCLC‑based analysis and performed overall survival analyses in a publicly available SCLC RNA‑seq cohort (PMID: 38181741). In the full SCLC cohort, higher KDM1A (LSD1) expression was significantly associated with shorter overall survival, supporting the prognostic relevance of LSD1 (revised Fig. 9l). By contrast, lower INSM1 expression showed a trend toward improved survival that did not reach statistical significance in the overall cohort (revised Fig. 9l).
To meet the request for subtype‑restricted evaluation, we further analyzed the SCLC‑A subgroup (defined by an ASCL1‑high transcriptional program aligned with current consensus). Directionally similar trends were observed for KDM1A and INSM1, but associations did not reach statistical significance, likely reflecting limited power within subtype‑restricted strata (revised Fig. 9m).
These findings are directionally concordant with prior pathology‑based reports linking lower INSM1/LSD1 expression to better outcomes in SCLC, while differences in cohort composition and therapy may contribute to variability across studies. For transparency, we now restrict all clinical inferences to SCLC datasets. Analytic details were prespecified (median expression cut‑offs; Kaplan–Meier log‑rank tests; Cox proportional‑hazards models reporting hazard ratios with 95% CIs; multiple‑testing control as appropriate), and cohort size/event counts are reported in the figure legends and Methods sections. Although clinical prognostication is not the primary aim of this mechanistic study, future work—where feasible—could extend survival analyses to additional public SCLC resources (e.g., George et al., 2015; Nabet et al., 2024) to further refine the clinical implications of the INSM1–LSD1 axis.

(2) Figure 2B would be easier to interpret if the cell line subtypes were labeled.
(3) The in-text reference for Figure 2D arrives after the in-text reference for Figure 2E.
(4) Page 15, line 317 seems to contain a typographical error “and GSK2879552”.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the careful reading and helpful suggestions. All items have been corrected in the revised manuscript, as follows:
(1) “potentially” has been corrected to “potently” (p. 6, line 102).
(2) Cell‑line subtypes are now explicitly labeled in Fig. 2b (panel and legend) to improve interpretability.
(3) The in‑text figure citations have been reordered so that Fig. 2d is cited before Fig. 2e at first mention.
(4) The typographical error on p. 15, line 317 has been corrected (removal of the extraneous “and” before “GSK2879552”).
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author): LSD1 inhibitor, epigenetic targeting and mass spectrometry
In this manuscript, Machida et al. studied the therapeutic effect and understand the mechanism of the new LSD1 inhibitor TAS1440 in neuroendocrine SCLC. Earlier studies showed that LSD1 inhibition derepresses notch and TGFb signaling resulting in suppression of SCLC growth. This study presents the first development of a new LSD1 inhibitor, TAS1440 which is a histone H3 competitive inhibitor of LSD1. TAS1440 demonstrated superior antiproliferative activity in SCLC-A subtype cells and exhibited in vivo activity in subcutaneous xenograft models. Mechanistically, TAS effects are attributed to both direct inhibition of LSD1 enzymatic activity as well as disruption of LSD1-repressive complexes leading to coordinated regulation of histone modifications and activation of transcription factors INSM1 and SMAD2 which reprograms the NOTCH and TGFb tumor suppressor pathways. Further depletion of INSM1 resulted in the abrogation of TAS1440 effects, suggesting the dependency of INSM1 for TAS1440 functions.
This study is interesting as TAS has the dual function of inhibition of LSD1 enzymatic activity and disrupting LSD1 complexes and holds significant promise as a new targeted therapy for the SCLC-A subtype with high INSM1 expression. Data was generated rigorously using multiple cell lines and demonstrated the superior activity of TAS1440 than existing LSD1 inhibitors, and mechanistic studies were thoroughly conducted using RNA-seq of 22 cell lines, as well as ChIP-seq and mass spec studies and rigorous validation in multiple cell lines. The figures are good quality and easy to follow and the manuscript is well written.
However, there are several issues noted in the manuscript and several claims are overstated without concrete evidence. The novelty of the study is moderate as LSD1's role in SCLC, and the utility of other LSD1 inhibitors was thoroughly investigated, although these inhibitors are associated with significant toxicity. The authors claim that TAS1440 has high specificity, less off-target effects, and is a safer drug, which could be a breakthrough for this study. Unfortunately, there was not enough data presented to support this statement. Further the objective states the identification of chemoresistance drivers, however no such studies using chemoresistance cells were conducted. In vivo studies are preliminary in nature, and only one subcutaneous xenograft model was used.
Response: We are grateful to Reviewer #4 for their insightful comments emphasizing (i) firm evidence of on‑target engagement, (ii) the relative novelty of TAS1440 in the context of prior LSD1 inhibitors, and (iii) the need for broader in vivo support. Guided by these suggestions, we have added genetic and biochemical validation of TAS1440–LSD1 engagement, expanded comparative profiling vs. other inhibitors, and strengthened our in vivo dataset. We have also revised the text to avoid overstatement and to align claims with the new evidence. Please refer to our detailed responses below.
#4-1
The on-target specificity of the compound should be established using LSD1-KO cells. Further, it is not clear if TAS1440 directly interacts with LSD1. This can be done using biotin-labeled TAS-1440 and LSD1 protein using avidin pulldown.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s important comment regarding the on‑target specificity of TAS1440.
Genetic dependency: To directly assess target dependency, we generated CRISPR–Cas9 LSD1‑knockout (KO) derivatives of NCI‑H1417 and NCI‑H146 (revised Fig. 7a, b; Fig. S12a, b). Upon TAS1440 exposure, LSD1‑KO cells were completely refractory to growth inhibition, in contrast to parental controls (revised Fig. 7c; Fig. S12c), indicating that TAS1440’s antiproliferative activity is LSD1‑dependent.
As a selectivity benchmark, we compared SP2509, a reported LSD1 inhibitor with off‑target liabilities: SP2509 retained partial activity in LSD1‑KO cells, consistent with mixed LSD1‑dependent and ‑independent effects, whereas TAS1440 lost activity entirely in the absence of LSD1 (revised Fig. 7c; Fig. S12c), reinforcing high target specificity.
Transcriptomic concordance: RNA‑seq further supported on‑target engagement. In LSD1‑KO NCI‑H1417 cells reconstituted with empty vector, TAS1440 induced minimal differential expression (MA plot, revised Fig. 7k), whereas a broad transcriptional response was observed in LSD1‑WT cells (revised Fig. 7i).
GSEA/KEGG showed robust enrichment of TAS1440‑associated pathways—most notably TGF‑β and NOTCH signaling—in WT but substantially attenuated responses in KO‑empty cells (revised Fig. 7m).
Biochemical selectivity and mechanism: Using recombinant enzymes, TAS1440 inhibited LSD1 with an IC₅₀ of 4.8 nM, while showing minimal inhibition of LSD2, MAO‑A, MAO‑B, and a panel of chromatin regulators (HDAC1, DNMT1, PRMT4, SMYD2, JmjC demethylases), each with IC₅₀ > 10,000 nM (revised Fig. 2f, g; Fig. S4b). Substrate‑competition assays with biotinylated H3K4me1 peptide showed that increasing substrate concentration shifted the TAS1440 IC₅₀ to higher values (rightward shift), consistent with an H3‑competitive mechanism. By contrast, the covalent inhibitor ORY‑1001 displayed substrate‑insensitive IC₅₀ values, as expected for an irreversible FAD‑directed agent.
Structural evidence for direct binding: X‑ray co‑crystal analysis shows TAS1440 occupying the histone H3‑binding pocket of LSD1 (revised Fig. 5i), providing a structural rationale for both enzymatic inhibition and disruption of the LSD1–INSM1 complex. Molecular docking further supports stable interactions within the H3 groove and proximity to INSM1/SMAD2 interaction surfaces (revised Fig. 5g, h).
We appreciate the suggestion to use a biotin‑labeled TAS1440 for avidin pulldown. Given the narrow H3‑binding groove observed in the co‑crystal, appending a bulky biotin is likely to perturb binding geometry and underestimate affinity/engagement. In lieu of this, we provide orthogonal lines of evidence—genetic KO abrogation, biochemical selectivity and substrate competition, and direct co‑crystal structural data—collectively establishing on‑target engagement of TAS1440 with LSD1.
#4-2
In vivo studies are conducted using subcutaneous models which do not mimic the actual microenvironment. Only one xenograft model was used. Studies using orthotopic models of SCLC and syngenic models with intact immune systems should be conducted to establish the superior activity of TAS1440. Further, there are no PDX models were utilized to account for the heterogeneity of SCLC.
Response: We appreciate this important suggestion. In the revision, we have expanded the in vivo efficacy assessment beyond NCI‑H1417 to three additional SCLC‑A xenograft models (NCI‑H146, NCI‑H510A, and COR‑L51) and a INSM1 knockout (KO) NCI-H146 xenograft model. INSM1 wild type (WT) NCI-H146 xenografts were responsive to TAS1440, whereas INSM1 knockout (KO) NCI-H146 xenografts were non responsive (Fig. 9a-f); dose, schedule, sample size, randomization/blinding, and statistics are reported in the figure legends (revised Fig. 9), reinforcing subtype‑selective activity within SCLC‑A across multiple lines.
To address microenvironmental relevance, we have conducted an orthotopic study by implanting SCLC‑A cells into the lung parenchyma. TAS1440 treatment markedly lowered intrathoracic tumor burden. CT imaging revealed a 66.7% reduction in tumor area at the maximal radius (revised Fig.9k). These results are concordant with our subcutaneous data and support on‑target activity within the lung microenvironment. Methods for the orthotopic model (surgical procedure, imaging schedules, predefined endpoints, randomization/blinding) have been added to the revised manuscript.
With respect to immunocompetent (syngeneic) models, we have performed pilot implantations to explore drug evaluation in an intact immune context. Human‑derived SCLC cell lines failed to engraft in immunocompetent mouse strains, precluding assessment of TAS1440 activity—an outcome consistent with xenogeneic rejection. Accordingly, true syngeneic evaluation would require murine SCLC allografts or genetically engineered mouse model (GEMM)–derived lines (e.g., Rb1/Trp53 ± Rbl2 backgrounds) or de novo GEMM cohorts. Securing these resources, establishing colonies, and completing the necessary protocol amendments would exceed the current major‑revision timeline.
Regarding patient‑derived xenograft (PDX) models, we agree they would better capture inter‑patient heterogeneity; however, acquisition, engraftment, and stabilization of early‑passage SCLC PDXs likewise extend beyond the present revision. Accordingly, we have (i) added three additional subcutaneous models and the orthotopic pilot (above) and (ii) revised the Discussion to acknowledge these limitations and to outline next‑step studies in immunocompetent and PDX settings with prespecified pharmacodynamic endpoints (e.g., pathway engagement, antigen‑presentation markers) and objective tumor‑control readouts.
#4-3
There were no details provided pertaining to how the in vivo dose of TAS1440 was determined, what its MTD, MED. Concerning toxicity, it appears that this compound also reduces body weight, suspecting the potential toxicity of this compound. It is important to study whether this compound has any hematologic toxicity as commonly observed with other LSD1 inhibitors.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. In the current study, TAS1440 was administered orally (p.o.) at 16.7 mg/kg/day and 50 mg/kg/day, guided by preliminary tolerability/exposure data and commonly used preclinical dosing ranges for non‑covalent LSD1 inhibitors. These regimens were generally tolerated in CB17/Icr‑Prkdc^scid/CrlCrlj mice and produced consistent antitumor effects across multiple SCLC‑A xenograft models.
We did not conduct formal maximum tolerated dose (MTD) or minimum effective dose (MED) studies in this work. No overt clinical signs (e.g., skin lesions, lethargy, sudden death) were observed; however, we observed body‑weight loss in TAS1440‑treated cohorts (revised Fig. S18a-d), indicating the need for careful dose optimization to balance efficacy and tolerability in future studies. To address the reviewer’s question about hematologic toxicity, we added a peripheral blood analysis. Compared with vehicle, TAS1440 produced significant reductions in red cell parameters—RBC, hemoglobin, and hematocrit—while WBC and platelets showed no significant change at the tested doses/time point; MCV, MCH, and MCHC were likewise unchanged (Fig. R2 for reviewer). This pattern is consistent with a normocytic, normochromic anemia without leukopenia or thrombocytopenia under the present conditions.
Consistent with prior experience for reversible LSD1 inhibitors, hematologic toxicity has been documented clinically (e.g., CC‑90011: anemia 51.1%, thrombocytopenia 46.6%; Grade ≥ 3 in 13.6% and 19.3%, respectively; Rudin et al., J Thorac Oncol. 2023). These adverse events have generally been manageable with dose modification.
We have added these clarifications to the revised Discussion section and acknowledge the need for follow‑up toxicity profiling, including hematologic assessments and formal dose‑ranging studies, in future work.
#4-4
TAS has dual activity of LSD1 enzymatic inhibition and complex disruptor. However, it is essential to determine if the enzymatic activity is important for TAS effects. Efficacy and mechanistic studies need to be conducted using enzymatic dead mutant LSD1 (K661A) to ascertain whether enzymatic activity is essential for TAS1440 effects.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important, mechanistically focused suggestion. LSD1 contributes to SCLC biology via both canonical (enzymatic demethylation) and non‑canonical (scaffolding/complex‑forming) functions. To isolate the role of catalytic activity in TAS1440 responses, we engineered a catalytically inactive LSD1 mutant (K661A).
Genetic system and validation: Using CRISPR–Cas9, we ablated endogenous LSD1 and reconstituted NCI‑H1417 and NCI‑H146 with 3×FLAG–MYC–LSD1‑WT, 3×FLAG–MYC–LSD1‑K661A, or empty vector (EV). Immunoblotting confirmed increased global H3K4me1/2 in K661A‑expressing cells, consistent with loss of demethylase activity, and WT/K661A expression levels were matched by densitometry (revised Fig. 7a, b; Fig. S12a, b).
Proliferation rescue: Both WT and K661A partially restored proliferation in LSD1‑KO cells, with a smaller rescue by K661A, indicating that catalytic activity contributes to LSD1‑driven growth (revised Fig. 7e, f; Fig. S12e, f).
TAS1440 activity in WT vs. K661A: TAS1440 inhibited growth in both WT‑ and K661A‑expressing cells, showing that activity is not solely attributable to catalytic blockade. As expected, TAS1440 increased NOTCH1 and pSMAD2 was attenuated in K661A relative to WT (revised Fig. 7g, h). qPCR for canonical NOTCH/TGF‑β targets recapitulated these trends (revised Fig. 7i).
Transcriptomic profiling: TAS1440 elicited broader differential‑expression changes and NOTCH/TGF‑β enrichment in WT cells, whereas responses were blunted in K661A and minimal in EV (RNA‑seq; KEGG/GSEA; revised Fig. 7j–m).
Complex disruption: Co‑immunoprecipitation (co‑IP) showed that LSD1‑K661A retains binding to INSM1 and SMAD2, and TAS1440 disrupts these interactions in both WT and K661A contexts (revised Fig. 7n), supporting a catalysis‑independent complex‑disruptor component.
Conclusion: Collectively, these data indicate that LSD1 catalytic activity is required for the full extent of TAS1440‑induced transcriptional reprogramming and pathway activation, while disruption of LSD1‑containing repressive complexes provides a second, catalysis‑independent contribution–supporting a dual‑function mechanism.
#4-5
It is not clear how it is different from existing reversible noncovalent inhibitors such as SP2509.
Response: Thank you for raising this important question. To delineate how TAS1440 differs from existing reversible, non‑covalent LSD1 inhibitors, we benchmarked TAS1440 against SP2509 and CC‑90011 across orthogonal assays (cell growth, genetic dependency, transcriptomics, complex disruption, and structural modeling).
1) On‑target dependency and growth phenotype: Across a panel of SCLC cell lines (revised Fig. S3a), TAS1440 and CC‑90011 produced broadly similar antiproliferative profiles, with TAS1440 showing greater potency in several sensitive lines. By contrast, SP2509 induced broad cytotoxicity at higher concentrations. Consistent with reported off‑target liabilities, SP2509 retained partial activity in LSD1‑knockout cells, whereas TAS1440 activity was abolished in the absence of LSD1 (revised Fig. 7c, Fig. S12c), supporting tighter on‑target dependence for TAS1440.
2) Transcriptional programs and pathway activation: RNA‑seq of NCI‑H1417 and NCI‑H146 treated with five LSD1 inhibitors revealed distinct expression signatures among TAS1440, CC‑90011, and SP2509 (revised Fig. 4i, Fig. S6i). GSEA indicated that TAS1440 uniquely and robustly enriched NOTCH and TGF‑β pathways (Fig. R3 for reviewer), which was concordant with immunoblot evidence of stronger NOTCH1 and pSMAD2 induction by TAS1440 (revised Fig. 4j, k).
3) Disruption of LSD1 repressive complexes: Co‑immunoprecipitation showed that TAS1440 efficiently disrupted LSD1–INSM1, LSD1–SMAD2, LSD1–HDAC1, and LSD1–HDAC2, whereas SP2509 did not affect LSD1–INSM1 or LSD1–SMAD2 and instead selectively perturbed LSD1–RCOR1 (revised Fig. 5e, f), indicating a distinct complex‑disruption fingerprint.
4) Structural rationale: Docking placed TAS1440 within the histone H3‑binding pocket of LSD1, adjacent to surfaces implicated in INSM1/SMAD2 interactions, whereas SP2509 docked at a topologically distinct site (revised Fig. 5g, h), providing a plausible basis for the divergent functional effects.
Conclusion: Together, these data differentiate TAS1440 from SP2509 (and from CC‑90011) by (i) tighter on‑target dependence, (ii) dual NOTCH/TGF‑β pathway activation, and (iii) broader disruption of LSD1‑corepressor complexes, establishing a distinct pharmacologic profile among reversible, non‑covalent LSD1 inhibitors.
#4-6
Some of the data was generated using only one cell line, particularly Figure 4g,h,j,k. and 6d,e. This should be done using at least one more cell line.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion. In response, we have replicated each of the single–cell-line findings in at least one additional SCLC-A model to confirm reproducibility and generalizability, mapping directly to the figures noted in the comment (former Fig. 4g, h, j, k and 6d, e):
 In vitro signaling and rescue (former Fig. 4g, h, j, k–related assays): We have repeated the rescue experiments and the comparative analyses of NOTCH1 and pSMAD2 activation under different LSD1 inhibitors in NCI-H146 (revised Fig. S6g–j) and performed parallel rescue/drug-comparison assays in NCI-H510A, yielding results concordant with NCI-H1417 (revised Fig. S8a–g). Experimental conditions (doses/timepoints) were matched to the original assays.
 Epigenomics (mechanistic support): We have conducted ChIP-seq for H3K4me1/2/3 and H3K27ac in NCI-H146, which recapitulated the TAS1440-induced chromatin changes observed in NCI-H1417 (revised Fig. S11h–o).
 Assays corresponding to Fig. 6d, e (complex disruption/pathway readouts): We have reproduced the experiments underlying Fig. 6d, e in NCI-H146 (added in revised Fig. S11h–o, as noted in the legends) and observed the same direction and magnitude of effects as in NCI-H1417, including the expected complex-disruption and pathway-activation patterns with TAS1440.
 In vivo generalization (context): Beyond NCI-H1417, we have expanded xenograft efficacy to NCI-H146, NCI-H510A, COR-L51 and INSM1 knockout (KO) NCI-H146 xenografts; INSM1 wild type (WT) xenografts were responsive to TAS1440 (revised Fig. 9a-e; Fig. 9g and Fig. S18e, i), consistent with our initial H1417 findings (revised Fig. 9a) whereas INSM1 knockout (KO) NCI-H146 xenografts were non responsive (revised Fig. 9f); TAS1440 reduced tumor growth across all models (dose, schedule, sample size, randomization/blinding, and statistics in revised Fig. 9), supporting reproducibility within SCLC-A across independent lines.
For all new experiments, we now report biological replicates (n), error metrics, effect sizes with 95% CIs, and statistical tests in the figure legends and Methods sections.
Taken together, these additions directly address the request to verify key results in ≥1 additional cell line per assay and support the robustness of TAS1440’s effects across independent SCLC-A models.
#4-7
Authors claim that TAS1440 dissociates TFs such as INSM1 and SMAD2 from the LSD1 complex and synergistically promotes the activation of key signaling pathways such as NOTCH and TGF-b via epigenetic reprogramming. However, no data was provided to support this conclusion except cell viability data.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important comment. Beyond cell-viability assays, we now provide orthogonal evidence that TAS1440 disrupts the LSD1–INSM1/SMAD2 repressive complex and reactivates NOTCH and TGF-β via epigenetic reprogramming.
1) Direct complex dissociation (biochemistry/proteomics).
Exogenous co-immunoprecipitation in NCI-H1417 showed reduced co-precipitation of INSM1 and SMAD2 with LSD1 after TAS1440 (empty-vector–normalized densitometry; fold-decrease: INSM1 = 5.81, SMAD2 = 2.40; n=3; two-tailed paired t-test; INSM1: P=0.0015, SMAD2: P=0.046; revised Fig. 5e). Affinity-purification mass spectrometry of the LSD1 interactome further demonstrated loss of multiple nuclear cofactors, including epigenetic regulators; INSM1 and SMAD2 were among the dissociated interactors (log fold-change indicating decrease: INSM1 = –6.77, 2 SMAD2 = –5.13; revised Fig. 5c).
2) Genetic dependency (necessity/sufficiency).
• INSM1: siRNA knockdown in NCI-H1417/NCI-H510A significantly attenuated TAS1440 response (ΔGI%: H510A = 17.63%, n=4, two-tailed unpaired t-test, P=0.003; H1417 = 10.99%, n=4, P=0.025; revised Fig. S13j, k). Conversely, INSM1 overexpression in resistant non-NE lines (NCI-H211 [SCLC-P] and NCI-H196 [SMARCA4-deficient]) restored NE features and increased TAS1440 sensitivity (EC50 shift: H211 = 49.63%, n=4, P<0.0001; H196 = 22.66%, n=4, P<0.0001; revised Fig. S17a, b). RNA-seq in these OE models showed baseline repression of NOTCH/TGF-β programs by INSM1 (e.g., TGF-β GSEA NES: H196 = –1.36, P<0.001) and on-treatment reactivation with TAS1440 (NOTCH GSEA NES: H211 = 1.30, P<0.001; H196 = 1.40, P<0.001; ΔDEGs: H211 = 958; H196 = 2230; revised Fig. S17c–f).
• SMAD2.:siRNA knockdown in NCI-H1417/H146/H510A conferred resistance to TAS1440 (ΔGI%: H1417 = 36.57%, n=8, P<0.0001; H146 = 8.92%, n=4, P=0.005; H510A = 27.02%, n=4, P<0.0001; revised Fig. 4g; Fig. S6g; Fig. S8c), and blunted TAS1440-induced transcriptional changes (ΔDEGs: H1417 = 619; H146 = 350; revised Fig. S7b), with selective attenuation of TGF-β-responsive genes (e.g., GSEA NES in H1417 from 1.34 (P<0.001) to 1.11 (P=0.22); H146 from 1.65 (P<0.001) to 1.22 (P=0.10); revised Fig. S7c–f). Double knockdown (INSM1+SMAD2) produced near-complete resistance to TAS1440 (n=4; revised Fig. 8l; S13h) and loss of pathway induction by qPCR (n=3; revised Fig. 8m; S13i).
3) Epigenomic reprogramming (ChIP-seq/ChIP-qPCR).
In NCI-H1417, INSM1 depletion did not change H3K4me1/2/3 at TSSs, but significantly increased H3K27ac genome-wide (revised Fig. 8n), with increased H3K27ac and transcripts at NOTCH1 and TGFB2 (revised Fig. S8o–r). SMAD2 ChIP-qPCR showed enhanced occupancy at NOTCH1/TGFB2 specifically with TAS1440, exceeding other LSD1 inhibitors (n=3; revised Fig. 6h; Fig. S11g).
Conclusion: Taken together, these orthogonal datasets demonstrate that TAS1440 dissociates INSM1/SMAD2 from LSD1 and reactivates NOTCH and TGF-β through coordinated epigenetic reprogramming. We have added statistical details (n, tests, effect sizes, P values) and clarified figure references in the revised manuscript accordingly.
#4-8
Data shows that TAS dissociates LSD1 interaction with INSM1 and SMAD2. However, much of the studies are conducted with only INSM1 manipulation. It is not clear what is the role of SMAD2 in TAS actions.
Response: Thank you for this important comment. To define the role of SMAD2—beyond our INSM1 data—in mediating TAS1440 activity, we have performed complementary genetic, genomic, and epigenomic analyses across multiple SCLC-A models (NCI-H1417, NCI-H146, and NCI-H510A).
1) Genetic dependency (siRNA).
SMAD2 knockdown significantly reduced TAS1440 sensitivity in NCI-H146 and NCI-H510A, consistent with NCI-H1417 (revised Fig. S6g–h, S8e-f). We report biological replicates (n), effect sizes with 95% CIs, and two-sided tests in the figure legends.
2) Genomic occupancy (ChIP-qPCR).
Upon TAS1440 treatment, SMAD2 occupancy at the NOTCH1 and TGFB2 loci increased, and did so more prominently than with other reversible LSD1 inhibitors tested (revised Fig. 6h; Fig. S11g), indicating enhanced recruitment under TAS1440 exposure.
3) Transcriptomic response (RNA-seq).
In NCI-H1417 and NCI-H146, siSMAD2 blunted TAS1440‑induced differential expression (total DEGs, up + down): NCI‑H1417 1,789 → 1,170 and NCI‑H146 675 → 325 in siNC vs. siSMAD2 (revised Fig. S7b).
4) Genetic epistasis (double knockdown).
Dual INSM1+SMAD2 knockdown in NCI-H1417 and NCI-H146 conferred near-complete resistance to TAS1440 and abrogated induction of NOTCH/TGF-β signatures by qPCR (revised Fig. 8k–m; S13g–i).
Conclusion.
Across orthogonal assays, SMAD2 is required for the full transcriptional and phenotypic response to TAS1440—non-redundant yet cooperative with INSM1 following LSD1-complex disruption. We have added statistical details (n, tests, effect sizes, and FDR where applicable) and clarified figure references in the revised manuscript accordingly.
#4-9
IP data show that in addition to TAS, ORY-1001, and GSK2879552 also reduce the LSD1 interaction with INSM1 despite the latter being catalytic inhibitors. How do the authors explain this? How is TAS1440's superior activity justified here?
Response: Thank you for raising this important point. While our co-immunoprecipitation (IP) experiments show that several LSD1 inhibitors—including TAS1440, ORY-1001, and GSK2879552—can reduce the LSD1–INSM1 interaction, the extent of dissociation is dose-dependent and compound-specific. To create a fair comparison, we benchmarked all three agents at matched concentrations (100, 300, 500 nM) under identical lysis/wash conditions with input-normalized densitometry. TAS1440 produced greater complex disruption at lower concentrations (revised Fig. S10g–j), indicating superior potency for breaking the LSD1–INSM1 complex at equimolar exposure.
Mechanistic rationale: Our structural data place TAS1440 within the histone H3-binding pocket of LSD1 (revised Fig. 5i), in proximity to residues engaged by H3-like peptides and reported INSM1-contacting regions. This geometry provides a direct steric basis for antagonizing INSM1 binding. By contrast, ORY-1001 and GSK2879552 are FAD-directed covalent (catalytic-site) inhibitors that occupy a topologically shifted region with limited spatial overlap with the INSM1 interface; the observed reduction in co-precipitation with these covalent inhibitors is therefore plausibly indirect/allosteric and, in our hands, less efficient at equimolar doses.
Functional consequence: Consistent with stronger complex disruption, TAS1440 drives more robust downstream reprogramming—including NOTCH1 and pSMAD2 induction and NOTCH/TGF-β pathway enrichment—relative to comparator agents (revised Fig. 4j, k). Together, these data support a dual-function mechanism for TAS1440 (potent catalytic inhibition plus direct competition at/near the H3/INSM1 interface) that explains both its stronger complex dissociation and greater transcriptional effects.
We have clarified these points in the revised manuscript, including the matched-dose IP methodology, normalized quantification, and figure cross-references (revised Fig. S10g–j; Fig. 5i).
#4-10
Studies that address the molecular basis of resistance using INSM1-KO need to be verified using reexpression of INSM1 in INSM1-KO background and show that reinstating INSM1 expression restores TAS1440 efficacy.
Response: Thank you for this insightful suggestion. To directly test whether loss-of-function phenotypes in INSM1-KO cells are rescued by INSM1 re-expression, we performed add-back experiments in NCI-H1417 and NCI-H146.
 Re-expression system and controls: INSM1-KO cells were transduced with INSM1 or empty vector (EV) (revised Fig. 8k, l; Fig. S13g, h, with replicate details in the legends).
 Functional rescue of drug response: Upon ectopic INSM1 re-expression, TAS1440 sensitivity was restored toward parental levels in dose–response viability assays (revised Fig. 8l; Fig. S13h), whereas EV controls remained resistant. Effect sizes (e.g., EC50 shift/AUC change), n (biological replicates), and statistical tests are provided in the figure legends.
 Pharmacodynamic rescue: Consistently, qPCR (and immunoblot where applicable) demonstrated re-activation of NOTCH/TGF-β pathway targets in the reconstituted lines, concordant with recovery of on-target pharmacodynamic signaling (revised Fig. 8m; Fig. S13i).
These data indicate that INSM1 is required for the full TAS1440 response and that re-expression restores TAS1440 efficacy in the INSM1-KO background within the tested context, thereby validating the conclusions drawn from our INSM1-KO models.
#4-11
Figure 7I has no significance as this data was generated using NSCLC. I think this data can be removed from the manuscript as earlier studies have already demonstrated the LSD1 survival correlation in NSCLC.
Response: We agree that NSCLC survival data are not appropriate to support SCLC‑specific claims. Accordingly, we removed the NSCLC survival panel (former Fig. 7I) and now restrict clinical inference to SCLC datasets. As a replacement, we present overall survival (OS) analyses in a publicly available SCLC RNA‑seq cohort (PMID: 38181741). In the overall SCLC cohort, higher KDM1A expression was associated with shorter OS, supporting the prognostic relevance of LSD1, whereas lower INSM1 showed a trend toward improved OS that did not reach statistical significance. In SCLC‑A, the direction of associations was concordant but non‑significant, likely reflecting limited power in subtype‑restricted strata. These directions are in line with prior pathology‑based reports, while inter‑cohort differences in clinical background and therapy may contribute to variability across studies. We report hazard ratios with 95% CIs, log‑rank P values, the prespecified cut‑point, cohort size, and event counts in the revised figure legends and Methods sections (revised Fig. 9l-m).
#5-1
Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author): structural biology, may know medicinal chemistry
This manuscript describes a new LSD1 (histone demethylase) inhibitor and its potential pharmacological activity against a sub-type of small-cell lung cancer. The bottom line is that the LSD1 inhibitor disrupts the interaction between the demethylase and INSM1. In this way, this transcription factor looses its ability to function as a repressor of NOTCH and TGF-β signaling. These pathways are thereby activated and induce an epigenetic reprogramming that halts cell proliferation. The authors must be congratulated for the extensive amount of work that they describe in this submission. The experiments are extremely well illustrated and described by the narrative. My enthusiasm is, however, considerably decreased by the consideration that the manuscript almost ignores previous literature. TAS1440, the hereby reported inhibitor, is chemically very similar to CC-90011, a non covalent inhibitor described 15 years ago (10.1021/acs.jmedchem.0c00978) that was moved forwards to clinical trials (doi.org/10.1021/acs.jmedchem.3c02133). Moreover, there is already quite some literature describing the interplay between INSM1 and LSD1 in SCLC. For instance, doi.org/10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-16-3502 shows that inhibition of the LSD1-INSM1 interaction "inhibits expression of neuroendocrine-associated genes, such as ASCL1", anticipating the conclusion of this work. Similar conclusions were given in reference 10 whereas reference 24 demonstrates that "T-3775440 (an irreversible LSD1 inhibitor) blocks proliferation of SCLC cells in vitro and retards SCLC tumor growth in vivo. T-3775440 disrupts the interaction between LSD1 and the transcriptional repressor INSM1, thereby inhibiting expression of neuroendocrine-associated genes, such as ASCL1. INSM1 silencing phenocopies the effects of T-3775440 on gene expression and cell proliferation, consistent with the likelihood T-3775440 mediated its effects in SCLC by inhibiting INSM1". These are virtually the same take-home message offered by this manuscript. The relevance is this work is the demonstration that stratification of the cancer sub-type is critical and that the levels of ASCL1 can be prognostic. The manuscript rationalizes this phenomenon describing a plausible molecular mechanism.
Whether this manuscript meets the degree of novelty expected by the journal is an editorial decision. I recommend that the Authors extensively revise their manuscript highlighting their new findings while properly referring to and comparing with previous work whenever this is relevant. I think that it would be important to compare TAS1440 with CC-90011 with regard to their antiproliferative activity and cell-type selectivity. Given their structural similarity, it may well be possible that they behave the same or with only marginal differences.
Response: We thank the reviewer for underscoring two key points—(i) the extensive prior literature on LSD1–INSM1 biology and LSD1 inhibition in SCLC, and (ii) the need for an explicit, head-to-head comparison with CC-90011 given their chemical relatedness. We have revised the Introduction/Discussion to more fully cite and contextualize prior work (including studies demonstrating INSM1–LSD1 interplay and neuroendocrine gene repression), and we now provide the following side-by-side analyses.
Antiproliferative activity and subtype selectivity.
Across a panel of SCLC cell lines (revised Fig. S3a), TAS1440 and CC-90011 showed broadly similar inhibition profiles, with TAS1440 exhibiting greater potency in several SCLC-A–sensitive lines. Stratified analyses by molecular subtype indicate stronger activity in SCLC-A relative to non-A subtypes for both agents (summary statistics reported in the legend). In contrast, SP2509 displayed broad cytotoxicity at higher concentrations and retained residual activity in LSD1-KO cells (revised Fig. 7c; Fig. S12c), consistent with reported off-target liabilities.
Transcriptional programs and pathway activation.
RNA-seq in NCI-H1417 and NCI-H146 treated with five LSD1 inhibitors revealed distinct expression signatures among TAS1440, CC-90011, and SP2509 (revised Fig. 4i; Fig. S6i). GSEA showed that TAS1440 more robustly enriched NOTCH and TGF-β pathways (Fig. R3 for reviewer), concordant with stronger NOTCH1 and pSMAD2 induction by immunoblot (revised Fig. 4j, k).
Disruption of LSD1 repressive complexes.
Co-immunoprecipitation/immunoblotting (revised Fig. 5e, f) demonstrated that TAS1440 efficiently disrupts LSD1–INSM1, LSD1–SMAD2, LSD1–HDAC1, and LSD1–HDAC2 interactions. SP2509 left LSD1–INSM1/SMAD2 largely unaffected but perturbed LSD1–RCOR1, indicating a distinct complex-disruption fingerprint (matched-dose conditions and input-normalized densitometry are detailed in the legends).
Structural rationale.
Docking places TAS1440 within the histone H3-binding pocket of LSD1 (revised Fig. 5g, h), proximal to surfaces implicated in INSM1/SMAD2 engagement, providing a plausible steric basis for complex disruption. By contrast, SP2509 adopts a topologically distinct pose, consistent with its divergent functional effects and off-target profile.
Conclusion.
Together, these data position TAS1440—relative to CC-90011 and SP2509—as having tighter on-target dependence, more robust NOTCH/TGF-β pathway activation, and broader disruption of LSD1 corepressor complexes, while explicitly situating our findings within the prior SCLC LSD1–INSM1 literature highlighted by the reviewer.
We have updated the manuscript accordingly and report effect sizes, replicates, and statistics in the figure legends and Methods sections.
Ultimately, we would like to express our sincere gratitude to the editors and reviewers for their positive and constructive criticism. The manuscript has vastly benefited from your valuable and insightful comments and suggestions. We look forward to hearing from you and would be happy to address any further concerns, if required. We hope this further pushes the manuscript closer to publication in your esteemed journal.
